transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?

I came in because... well, because I keep hearing voices, and it’s gotten so clear that I can’t just brush it off anymore. It sounds like somebody is standing right there in my little studio with me, like not a thought in my head, not like remembering somebody’s voice — I mean clear, out loud, like a person in the room.

They’ll say my name, and then they’ll say things about my work being judged. And I’ll stop what I’m doing and look around, because it feels that real, but the house is quiet. Nobody’s there. I check, and there’s no one. It’s really upsetting because I’ll be trying to go about my day, and then there it is again, like I’m being watched or evaluated somehow. That’s what finally made me come in.
During the time you’ve been hearing the voices, have you also had a period when you felt unusually high, energized, or euphoric for days at a time?

Yes… yes, there was a stretch like that. I don’t know if I’d call it “high” exactly, but I was running on almost no sleep, just a few hours, and I felt like I had all this energy and this big purpose. I was pushing these big plans I had, like with my art and also care plans, like I was going to organize everything and make something really important out of it.

And during that same time, the voices were happening in the studio too. I’d be in there working, barely sleeping, feeling like I had to keep going, and I’d hear them so clearly. And I also felt really certain that people were watching my work somehow, like it was being monitored or judged. It all kind of came together at the same time, the energy and the not sleeping and the voices.
Have you ever heard the voices during a time when your mood felt normal?

Yes. That’s actually part of what scares me, because it wasn’t only when I had all that energy and wasn’t sleeping.

There was a time after that, when I kind of came down from it — like my energy dropped back down and I was sleeping more like my usual amount again — and I thought maybe the voices would stop because I wasn’t in that keyed-up state anymore. But they didn’t. They kept going. I’d be feeling more normal, not all revved up, just trying to go through my regular day, and I’d still hear them.

And it wasn’t just for a day or two. It went on for several weeks. I’d be in my studio or around my things, and the voices would still come, and I still had that feeling that my work was being judged or tracked somehow. I remember thinking, “Why is this still happening if I’m sleeping again?” because I wanted to believe it was just from being overtired, but it kept happening even when my mood felt more normal.
Have you had a period when you felt depressed most of the day nearly every day for at least two weeks?

I’m not really sure how to answer that. I mean, I’ve had days where I’ve felt low or worn down by everything, like just tired of dealing with it, but I don’t know if it was most of the day nearly every day for two whole weeks.

When you say depressed, do you mean like crying all the time, or not wanting to get out of bed, or just feeling heavy and discouraged? Because I can get discouraged, definitely, but I haven’t really kept track of it in a neat way like that. I don’t want to say yes if I’m not sure.
Have you ever had a time when you felt depressed most of the day nearly every day for at least two weeks?

I still don’t know that I can say it that clearly, like “yes, for two weeks.” I’ve had low times, and I’ve had times where I felt worn out and kind of defeated, but I wasn’t marking it on a calendar, you know?

Some days I’d feel heavy and discouraged for a big part of the day, and then maybe the next day I’d be more distracted or just trying to get through things. So I don’t want to tell you something wrong. When you say “most of the day nearly every day,” that sounds very specific, and I’m not sure I can honestly say I’ve had that for at least two weeks straight. I just know I’ve had periods where I felt really down and tired of everything, but I can’t pin it down the way you’re asking.
Before the voices started, had you been using drugs or substances that can affect the mind, like meth, cocaine, LSD, or a lot of cannabis?

I’m not really sure how to answer that exactly. I mean, I know what you’re asking, like whether something I took could have set it off, but I don’t want to say something wrong.

I wasn’t sitting there thinking, “Oh, this started right after some drug,” if that’s what you mean. I don’t really have a clear connection in my mind like that. And some of those things you listed, I’d have to be honest, I don’t really know all the categories or what counts as “a lot” with something like cannabis. I know people talk about substances like it’s very obvious, but for me I’m trying to think back to before the voices started and it’s kind of blurry in the sense of what mattered and what didn’t.

So… I can’t really point to meth or cocaine or LSD or heavy marijuana use and say, yes, that was happening before the voices. I just don’t have that to tell you. If there’s something specific you want me to go through, I can try, but I don’t remember it being tied to something like that.
Has a doctor ever told you that you have a brain or neurological condition?

Not that I know of. I mean, I don’t remember any doctor sitting me down and saying, “You have a brain condition” or “You have a neurological condition,” like something with the nerves or the brain itself.

I’ve been to doctors for different things over the years, but if you mean like a diagnosis from a neurologist or something like that, I don’t think so. Sometimes medical words go by fast and I don’t always know what category they’re putting things in, so I don’t want to say absolutely never if it’s written somewhere and I didn’t understand it. But as far as what I’ve been told directly, no, I haven’t been told I have something like that.
Did the voices start all of a sudden, within a couple of days?

I’m not sure I can say it was all of a sudden like that, like within just a couple of days. I don’t have it organized in my head that neatly.

When I think back on it, it’s hard to separate what started when, because at first I don’t know if I was even understanding what was happening. It wasn’t like I wrote down, “This is day one.” I just remember becoming aware of it, and then looking back and wondering if it had been creeping in before I really admitted it to myself.

So if you mean did I wake up one day and then two days later it was clearly there, I can’t honestly say that. I don’t know. It feels more blurry than sudden to me, but I don’t want to make it sound like I’m sure about the timeline when I’m not.
Did the voices continue for at least one month?

Yes… yes, they did. It’s been way longer than a month.

I mean, the voices and the fears I have about my work being watched, that’s been going on for about nine months now. It’s hard for me to say it like a clean start date, like I said before, but once it was happening, it didn’t just stop after a few days or a couple weeks. It kept going.

And I know a month is what you’re asking, but in my head it feels like it’s taken up such a big stretch of time that I almost lose track of how long it’s been. But yes, definitely at least a month. More like around nine months.
Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks when you felt depressed most of the day nearly every day?

I don’t really know how to answer that cleanly. I’ve definitely had times where I felt really low, like heavy and worn down, and it can feel like it’s on me for a while. But if you’re asking specifically, like, two full weeks where it was most of the day, nearly every day… I’m not sure I’ve kept track of it that way.

Sometimes the days kind of run together, and I don’t always notice until later that I’ve been feeling bad for a stretch. But I don’t want to say yes if I can’t honestly remember it being that exact kind of pattern. I guess I’d say I’m not sure.
Have you ever had a time when you lost interest or pleasure in almost everything for at least two weeks?

I’m not really sure. I know there are times where things don’t feel enjoyable like they used to, but I don’t know if I can say it was almost everything, for at least two weeks, in that clear way.

Like, sometimes I’ll stop wanting to do things, or I just don’t feel much from them, but then I don’t know if that’s because I’m tired, or stressed, or just not in the mood. I don’t keep track day by day, so when you ask “two weeks,” I start trying to count it in my head and it gets kind of foggy.

So I don’t want to say yes if I’m not sure. I guess the honest answer is I don’t know if it’s been that specific.
During those low periods, did you ever feel sad or down most of the day nearly every day?

I don’t know if I can say it was most of the day nearly every day. I mean, I’ve had times where I felt down, yes, like emotionally tired and kind of weighed down, but when you say “most of the day” and “nearly every day,” I start second-guessing myself.

Some days I might wake up feeling bad and it stays with me, but other days it kind of comes and goes, or I get distracted by what I have to do. And then later I’ll think, “Was I sad all day, or was I just overwhelmed?” It’s hard for me to separate it out like that.

So I guess the honest answer is I’m not sure. I know I’ve had low periods, but I can’t clearly remember if it was sad or down most of the day nearly every day.
Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks when you felt hopeless nearly every day?

I don’t know if I can answer that as a clear yes. Hopeless is a strong word, and I’m trying to think if there was a stretch where I felt that way nearly every day for two weeks straight, but I don’t really keep track of my feelings in that kind of calendar way.

I’ve had times where things felt really hard, like I couldn’t see my way through them, but then there might be moments where I’m just numb, or distracted, or getting through work or whatever I have to do. So I don’t know if that counts as hopeless nearly every day, or if it was more like feeling worn down and stuck.

I guess what I can say is I’ve felt low at times, but I’m not sure about a two-week period of feeling hopeless nearly every day.
Have you ever gone through a time when you were crying much more than usual?

I don’t really know. I mean, I’ve cried at times, sure, but “much more than usual” is hard for me to judge, because I’m not someone who keeps track of that. Sometimes I’ll tear up when I’m alone or when I’m just overwhelmed, but then other times I kind of hold it in, especially around people, because I don’t like feeling watched or having to explain myself.

So if you’re asking was there a clear period where I was crying all the time or noticeably more than normal, I’m not sure I can say that. I don’t remember it in a clear way like, “yes, this week or those weeks I cried every day.” It’s more blurry than that. I know I’ve had emotional moments, but I don’t know if it was much more than usual.
Was there ever a period of at least two weeks when you were hearing the voices even though you were not having a high-energy or depressed mood episode?

Yes, I think so. There was a time like that, where the high-energy part had kind of settled down already. Like I wasn’t running around with all that extra energy anymore, and my sleep had gone more back to normal — I was sleeping more regular again, not like before.

But even after that, the voices didn’t just stop. They kept going for a while, like several weeks. And it wasn’t like I was in one of those really low times either, at least not that I can clearly say. I wasn’t feeling especially up or especially depressed the whole time, but I was still hearing them.

And along with that, I still had this feeling — or belief, I guess — that people were judging me or watching how I was doing my work, like tracking what I was doing. It felt like they were paying attention to me in a way that wasn’t normal. That kept going even after my mood and sleep seemed more normal. So yes, there was a stretch where those things were still happening on their own.
Have you ever had a time when, for two weeks in a row, you felt depressed nearly every day?

I’m not really sure how to answer that one clearly. I’ve had times where I felt down, like really heavy and worn out inside, but when you say “for two weeks in a row” and “nearly every day,” I get stuck because I don’t remember it in that exact kind of way.

There have been stretches where I wasn’t myself, where getting through the day felt harder and I didn’t feel good emotionally, but I don’t know if I would call it depressed every single day, or almost every day, for a full two weeks. Some days I might feel low, and then another day I’m more just numb or distracted or trying to do what I have to do.

So I guess my honest answer is I don’t know. I can’t say yes for sure, but I also don’t want to say no like I’ve never felt depressed. I just can’t pin it down to that two-week period the way you’re asking.
Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks when you lost interest or pleasure in nearly all activities?

I don’t know if I can say that exactly. I mean, I’ve had times where I didn’t feel like doing much, where things just felt kind of flat or like too much effort, but “nearly all activities” for two weeks straight… I’m not sure.

Like, I might stop doing certain things for a while, or I’ll just go through the motions, but I don’t always know if that means I lost interest or if I was just tired, stressed, or trying to get through the day. Sometimes I still do things because I have to, not because I’m enjoying them, but I don’t really keep track of when that starts or how long it lasts.

So I guess I can’t give you a clear yes. I’ve had periods where I wasn’t enjoying things the way I normally would, but I don’t know if it was nearly everything for at least two weeks.
Have you ever had a time when, for at least two weeks, you felt no pleasure in things you usually enjoy?

Yes… I think that’s probably closer to what happens with me. Like, when I’m not all wound up or going nonstop, I can just kind of sit there and nothing feels worth doing.

I’ll have my coffee in the morning, and I mean I’ll just sit there so long it gets cold, and I don’t even care enough to warm it back up. My phone will ring or people will call, and I’ll look at it and just not answer. Not even because I’m busy, just because I don’t feel like talking or getting into anything.

And things I usually do like… like the walking club, I’ll just stop going. I know it would probably be good for me to get out, and normally I like seeing people there, but in those times I just don’t care enough to make myself go. Same with painting. I can have my paintbrush right there, and I won’t even pick it up. It’s not even like I’m thinking, “Oh, I hate this now.” It’s more like there’s no pull toward it, no enjoyment waiting for me in it.

So yes, I guess there have been times like that, where things I usually enjoy just don’t feel like anything to me.
During one of those times when nothing felt enjoyable, did that loss of pleasure last for at least two weeks?

I’m not completely sure. I want to say maybe, because it feels like those stretches go on and on when I’m in them, but I don’t sit there marking the calendar, you know? I don’t always know if it was exactly two weeks or if it was like ten days, or if it kind of faded in and out.

When I’m like that, the days sort of blend together. I’ll know I’ve missed the walking club more than once, and I’ll know the painting stuff has been sitting there untouched, and I’ll know I haven’t been answering people much. But then if you ask me, “Was it fourteen days straight?” I get nervous answering because I don’t want to say it wrong.

So… I know it lasts more than just a day or two. It’s not just a bad afternoon. But whether it was at least two full weeks, I honestly can’t say for sure.
Have you ever had a time when you felt down or depressed nearly every day for two weeks in a row?

I don’t know that I can answer that cleanly. I mean, I’ve definitely had times where I felt low, like heavy or just… not myself, and it felt like it was there most days. But when you say “nearly every day for two weeks in a row,” that’s where I get stuck, because I don’t always track it that way.

Some days I might feel really down in the morning and then be a little better later, or I might keep moving because I have to, even if inside I feel kind of sunk down. And then I wonder, does that count as depressed nearly every day? Or does it only count if I’m crying or can’t function? I’m not trying to dodge the question, I just don’t want to say yes if I’m not sure it was exactly like that.

So… I’ve had stretches where my mood was bad for more than just a day or two, definitely. But whether it was two full weeks in a row, nearly every day, I’m not completely sure.

doctor.intent: Open the interview by inviting the patient to describe their main concern in their own words
doctor.question: Hi, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?

target_item.name: Hallucinations
target_item.manifestation: I came in because I keep hearing voices clear as somebody standing in my little studio, saying my name and telling me my work is being judged, even when the house is quiet and nobody is there.
target_item.reason: This is the first reply of the consultation, so I must return the chief complaint symptom code, which is S020.

patient.answer:
I came in because... well, because I keep hearing voices, and it’s gotten so clear that I can’t just brush it off anymore. It sounds like somebody is standing right there in my little studio with me, like not a thought in my head, not like remembering somebody’s voice — I mean clear, out loud, like a person in the room.

They’ll say my name, and then they’ll say things about my work being judged. And I’ll stop what I’m doing and look around, because it feels that real, but the house is quiet. Nobody’s there. I check, and there’s no one. It’s really upsetting because I’ll be trying to go about my day, and then there it is again, like I’m being watched or evaluated somehow. That’s what finally made me come in.

inference.note: Initial differential based on clear auditory hallucinations with possible persecutory/evaluative content. Added primary psychotic disorders (schizophrenia, delusional disorder, acute/transient psychotic disorder, schizoaffective disorder) and secondary causes (organic psychosis, substance-induced psychotic disorder). No evidence yet to narrow further.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there are prominent mood episodes alongside the hallucinations, to distinguish a primary psychotic disorder from schizoaffective disorder.
doctor.question: During the time you’ve been hearing the voices, have you also had a period when you felt unusually high, energized, or euphoric for days at a time?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: When I was sleeping only a few hours and pushing my big art-and-care plans, I was also hearing the voices in the studio and feeling certain people were watching my work.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the hearing voices occurred during the same period as unusually high or energized mood, which directly concerns psychotic symptoms and manic episode occurring concurrently.

patient.answer:
Yes… yes, there was a stretch like that. I don’t know if I’d call it “high” exactly, but I was running on almost no sleep, just a few hours, and I felt like I had all this energy and this big purpose. I was pushing these big plans I had, like with my art and also care plans, like I was going to organize everything and make something really important out of it.

And during that same time, the voices were happening in the studio too. I’d be in there working, barely sleeping, feeling like I had to keep going, and I’d hear them so clearly. And I also felt really certain that people were watching my work somehow, like it was being monitored or judged. It all kind of came together at the same time, the energy and the not sleeping and the voices.

inference.note: Concurrent auditory hallucinations/paranoid ideas with a period of decreased need for sleep, high energy, and expansive/goal-directed plans makes a mood-related psychosis more likely, so F25.9 rises to the top; isolated delusional disorder (F22) is less likely because there are prominent hallucinations and mood symptoms.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the psychotic symptoms ever occurred outside of mood episodes, which is key to distinguishing schizoaffective disorder from bipolar disorder with psychotic features and related psychotic disorders.
doctor.question: Have you ever heard the voices during a time when your mood felt normal?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 3
target_item.manifestation: There was a time after my energy dropped and I was sleeping more normally when the voices and the belief that people were judging or tracking my work kept going for several weeks.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the voices occurred when mood was normal, which directly relates to psychotic symptoms persisting outside a major mood episode.

patient.answer:
Yes. That’s actually part of what scares me, because it wasn’t only when I had all that energy and wasn’t sleeping.

There was a time after that, when I kind of came down from it — like my energy dropped back down and I was sleeping more like my usual amount again — and I thought maybe the voices would stop because I wasn’t in that keyed-up state anymore. But they didn’t. They kept going. I’d be feeling more normal, not all revved up, just trying to go through my regular day, and I’d still hear them.

And it wasn’t just for a day or two. It went on for several weeks. I’d be in my studio or around my things, and the voices would still come, and I still had that feeling that my work was being judged or tracked somehow. I remember thinking, “Why is this still happening if I’m sleeping again?” because I wanted to believe it was just from being overtired, but it kept happening even when my mood felt more normal.

inference.note: Psychotic symptoms persisted for several weeks when mood was normal, which strongly supports a schizoaffective picture; manic symptoms point specifically toward F25.0. This makes pure mood-congruent psychosis less likely and narrows from broad prior options by prioritizing schizoaffective disorder, manic type.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a depressive episode lasting at least two weeks, but the provided symptom profile does not include a depressive mood symptom or major depressive episode item.

I’m not really sure how to answer that. I mean, I’ve had days where I’ve felt low or worn down by everything, like just tired of dealing with it, but I don’t know if it was most of the day nearly every day for two whole weeks.

When you say depressed, do you mean like crying all the time, or not wanting to get out of bed, or just feeling heavy and discouraged? Because I can get discouraged, definitely, but I haven’t really kept track of it in a neat way like that. I don’t want to say yes if I’m not sure.

I still don’t know that I can say it that clearly, like “yes, for two weeks.” I’ve had low times, and I’ve had times where I felt worn out and kind of defeated, but I wasn’t marking it on a calendar, you know?

Some days I’d feel heavy and discouraged for a big part of the day, and then maybe the next day I’d be more distracted or just trying to get through things. doctor.intent: Determine whether the psychosis could be substance-induced, which would distinguish F19.5 from primary psychotic or schizoaffective disorders.
doctor.question: Before the voices started, had you been using drugs or substances that can affect the mind, like meth, cocaine, LSD, or a lot of cannabis?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about drug or substance use as a possible cause of the voices, but the provided symptom profile does not include any substance use item.

patient.answer:
I’m not really sure how to answer that exactly. I mean, I know what you’re asking, like whether something I took could have set it off, but I don’t want to say something wrong.

I wasn’t sitting there thinking, “Oh, this started right after some drug,” if that’s what you mean. I don’t really have a clear connection in my mind like that. And some of those things you listed, I’d have to be honest, I don’t really know all the categories or what counts as “a lot” with something like cannabis. I know people talk about substances like it’s very obvious, but for me I’m trying to think back to before the voices started and it’s kind of blurry in the sense of what mattered and what didn’t.

So… I can’t really point to meth or cocaine or LSD or heavy marijuana use and say, yes, that was happening before the voices. I just don’t have that to tell you. If there’s something specific you want me to go through, I can try, but I don’t remember it being tied to something like that.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the psychotic symptoms could be due to a medical or neurological condition, helping distinguish an organic psychosis from primary psychotic disorders.
doctor.question: Has a doctor ever told you that you have a brain or neurological condition?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a brain or neurological condition, but the symptom profile does not include any item covering neurological or medical diagnoses.

patient.answer:
Not that I know of. I mean, I don’t remember any doctor sitting me down and saying, “You have a brain condition” or “You have a neurological condition,” like something with the nerves or the brain itself.

I’ve been to doctors for different things over the years, but if you mean like a diagnosis from a neurologist or something like that, I don’t think so. Sometimes medical words go by fast and I don’t always know what category they’re putting things in, so I don’t want to say absolutely never if it’s written somewhere and I didn’t understand it. But as far as what I’ve been told directly, no, I haven’t been told I have something like that.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the psychosis began suddenly, which would help distinguish an acute/transient psychotic disorder from schizophrenia-spectrum or schizoaffective disorders.
doctor.question: Did the voices start all of a sudden, within a couple of days?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the suddenness/onset timing of the voices within a couple of days, but the symptom profile only covers presence and overall duration of hallucinations, not whether they began abruptly.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure I can say it was all of a sudden like that, like within just a couple of days. I don’t have it organized in my head that neatly.

When I think back on it, it’s hard to separate what started when, because at first I don’t know if I was even understanding what was happening. It wasn’t like I wrote down, “This is day one.” I just remember becoming aware of it, and then looking back and wondering if it had been creeping in before I really admitted it to myself.

So if you mean did I wake up one day and then two days later it was clearly there, I can’t honestly say that. I don’t know. It feels more blurry than sudden to me, but I don’t want to make it sound like I’m sure about the timeline when I’m not.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether the psychotic symptoms lasted at least one month, which best separates schizophrenia from brief/acute psychotic disorder and helps refine schizoaffective vs schizophrenia-spectrum diagnoses.
doctor.question: Did the voices continue for at least one month?

So yes, I guess there have been times like that, where things I usually enjoy just don’t feel like anything to me.
